newsitem.title: INDIA: India Maruti profit up, but repeat seen difficult.
newsitem.headline: India Maruti profit up, but repeat seen difficult.

text.p: India's largest car maker Maruti Udyog Ltd on Monday announced a 17 percent rise in profit for 1996/97 (April-March), but cautioned that it would be tough to maintain the pace of growth in the coming year.

"Next year we have a difficult task of how to maintain our profit rather than increase it. We will do our best to see that our profit levels do not decline," managing director R.C. Bhargava told a news conference.
The company's profit after tax rose to 5.01 billion rupees ($139.56 million) in 1996/97 from 4.28 billion in the previous year, riding a 23 percent surge in sales.
The firm, a 50-50 joint venture between Japan's Suzuki Motor Corp and the Indian government, said vehicle sales rose to 338,690 in 1996/97 from 275,411 in the previous year.

Maruti said production would increase marginally to 340,000 vehicles, and a small increase in exports to 38,000 vehicles was planned. But the plant was already running at peak level, and a substantial hike in output was difficult, it said.
Bhargava said the firm would focus on trimming costs, rather than boosting sales, to strengthen its performance in 1997/98.
"I think we can sell more, but we don't have the (production) capacity," he said.
Suzuki and the Indian government are locked in a tussle on funding a proposed expansion.
The government is reluctant to endorse Suzuki's move to raise its equity, which many analysts see as an effort by the Japanese firm to hike its stake and control over the firm.

Maruti officials said the firm has pinned its hopes on sales of its 800-cc hatchback model -- which commands more than 80 percent of the segment of India's automobile market -- after fast-growing competition in the larger car segments had eaten into sales of its 1,300-cc Esteem model.
Esteem's sales plunged to about 23,000 cars in 1996/97 from nearly 40,000 in the previous year, and its market share dropped to less than 40 percent from 68 percent, they said.

Many foreign car makers, including Korea's Daewoo Corp, Germany's Daimler Benz, and U.S.-based General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co set up joint ventures to make bigger cars after India allowed them in under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.
"I see very small growth in the larger car segment in the years to come," Bhargava said in response to a question on the Esteem's future.

"All the competition is in this area only. There are no new roads, the highways are clogged and dangerous, there is no parking space available. Why would anyone want to buy a big car?" ($1 = 35.90 rupees)
